analysis.one_liner: Pays Medicare doctors based on the resources each service takes, not customary charges, and caps extra billing.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: referred to two House committees in June 1989, it received no markup and no vote before Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare then paid doctors based on each doctor's own 'usual and customary' charges, which meant the same office visit could be paid very differently depending on the doctor. This bill would have phased in, from 1990 to 1993, a fee schedule built from the actual resources each service takes — the doctor's time, staff, and office costs — raising pay for office visits and primary care while lowering it for procedures. To keep total Medicare doctor spending level, cuts in one area paid for raises in another. It also barred paying more simply because the doctor is a specialist, and capped what non-participating doctors could charge patients above Medicare's approved amount at 120 percent of the fee schedule.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially those treated by doctors who do not accept Medicare assignment, because the bill would cap extra-billing at 120 percent of the fee schedule amount. Primary care doctors would also gain, since the relative-value weights would pay more for evaluation and management services like office visits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries and primary care doctors

how_it_helps.text: Replaces payment based on doctors' own prevailing and customary charges with a fee schedule based on the relative resources used for each service, phased in from 1990 to 1993.
Bars the Secretary from varying a service's relative value based on whether the physician is a specialist, so the same service is paid the same regardless of who performs it.

Phases in, from 1991 to 1993, a limit on nonparticipating physicians' actual charges to 120 percent of the fee schedule amount, which restricts how much doctors can bill patients above Medicare's approved payment.
Keeps the transition budget neutral: the conversion factor is set so aggregate payments each year match what they would have been under the old system, so the reform costs Medicare nothing overall.
Factors malpractice expenses into the relative value of each service as a separate component, with its own geographic adjustment.

analysis.who_pays: Procedural specialists — surgeons, radiologists, and other doctors whose services would be paid less under resource-based weights — because the budget-neutral design funds the primary care raises by trimming payments for procedures. The nonparticipating physicians facing the 120 percent charge cap also give up unlimited extra billing.

drawbacks.text: Because the fee schedule is budget neutral, higher pay for office visits must be offset by lower pay for procedures and specialty services, which opponents of resource-based payment argued could discourage access to specialty care.

The bill bars administrative and judicial review of the relative values, national conversion factors, geographic indices, and fee schedule area selections, so affected physicians would have no appeal route to challenge the rates.

The 120 percent cap on actual charges for nonparticipating physicians limits their billing flexibility and, from 1993, applies to the full fee schedule amount rather than a blend with prevailing charges.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The redesign is broadly fair: it pays for the actual work and resources behind each service instead of legacy charge histories, and the budget-neutral structure means no new federal cost. The real tradeoffs are that specialists take the offsetting pay cuts and that the bill strips judicial review of the rates, concentrating rate-setting power in the Secretary. On balance, the beneficiary protections — especially the limit on extra billing — outweigh those costs.

outcome.mechanism: Waxman introduced it in June 1989 and it was sent to two committees — Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce — where it went to health subcommittees; neither advanced it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on June 14, 1989, and it was referred jointly to the House Committees on Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce.
It was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health on June 19 and to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on July 5.
No further action appears in the record: neither committee held a markup, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor among the House's 257 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody ultimately kept the policy off the books: months after this bill stalled, Congress enacted a resource-based Medicare physician fee schedule in the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989, so the same payment overhaul became law that year through a different vehicle. This bill's quiet death mainly cost time and left its specific balance-billing provisions behind.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody, ultimately; the reform passed that year anyway

for.name: Rep. Henry A. Waxman
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA); bill sponsor and chairman of the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare resource-based fee schedule bill and referred it jointly to two committees.

against.name: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a markup in the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare physician payment; the record shows no action after subcommittee referral.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a markup in the second committee of referral; the record shows no action after subcommittee referral.

against.name: Specialty physician societies
against.role: National medical associations representing procedure-heavy specialties
against.what_they_did: Opposed replacing charge-based Medicare payment with a resource-based scale that would cut payments for procedures, pushing instead for a scale weighted toward their members' services.

sides.party_line_note: There were no floor votes and only one cosponsor, so the record shows no measurable partisan split — the bill simply stalled in committee.

industries.note: The bill pays each service by its resource cost, so surgery, imaging, and other procedures would be paid less while the aggregate total stays level. Because specialists' extra fees came out of Medicare patients' and taxpayers' pockets under the old charge-based system, their interest ran against beneficiaries here.

Evaluation and management services — office visits, hospital visits, consultations — would be paid more under relative-value weights reflecting time and effort, and the bill requires coding that differentiates them by time spent. Their gain came alongside better-protected Medicare patients.
